The git adapter keeps `melian/state`, commits built with git's plumbing and never a checkout, `--force-with-lease` with backoff, and a wall-clock deadline; a record is a plain JSON file, and one commit holds a batch. A record that cannot fit even so fails the guardrails check, and the review reads not reviewed, by the maintainer's ruling that [the decision](decisions/2026-11-20-guardrails-record-fits-the-store.md) records. It builds commits in a bare repository of its own beside the clone, `records.git`, and fetches the branch's whole history into it. A file Melian did not write refuses work on the changeset whose folder holds it, or all work when it sits anywhere else, by [the amending decision](decisions/2026-11-14-git-record-store-refuses-by-location.md). A record counts because the store accepted it, so the store's write access is the trust, and no writer holds a key; a repository with `trust.writers: false`, or one that takes pull requests from forks, pins the trusted host's one key, and a store that is no branch of the repository is trusted only when the base's policy writes that out. In CI, a job that ran a head's code hands its records to one that ran none, which adds only the kinds a review writes, so a head's code can never dismiss. A fork's head hands over only the results of checks that run its code, today `static.mutation` alone, and the job that holds the key writes the fork's account and round itself, as [the account record decision](decisions/2026-11-16-account-record.md) records. An account names the resolution policy its round was decided under by fingerprint, and a reader decides the round only under that policy: under another, or with none, or for an account that names none or predates the field, the round reads not reviewed, as [its amendment](decisions/2026-11-16-account-names-its-resolution-policy.md) records. A record written before Melian withheld outside text fails its payload check, so a store that holds one fails its checks until the record is removed, as [the later amendment](decisions/2026-11-18-records-before-withheld-text-are-refused.md) records. A result's key is the hash of the whole request its producer was given, so no key can leave out an input. Core's `KeyedRequest` builds that key, and triage, check runs, verification and walkthroughs use it, as [the request keys decision](decisions/2026-11-14-request-keys-as-built.md) records; the lens run follows. Another host resumes by building its own requests, importing the records whose keys match, and running only what lacks one. A mutation run is the exception: the head's tests can read `PATH`, `HOME` and `TMPDIR`, which no key holds. So the record carries it for the round that read it, and only the host that ran it reuses it for a run of its own. The maintainer ruled so on 2026-11-15, as [the amendment](decisions/2026-11-15-check-run-keys-lang-under-mutation.md) records. Nothing in the store is secret: a marker is proved by a value whose hash the publisher recorded before posting. So a record carries no text a tool, a provider or the head's code wrote, by [the outside-text decision](decisions/2026-11-16-shared-records-carry-no-outside-text.md). A failed check's error, a skip's reason, a note or a caveat reads as a fixed sentence, while the full text stays in the reviewing host's own store and terminal. Once a changeset's records are in the store, everything local is cache.

snippet.text: `RelayBatch` in `src/record-relay.ts` reads the directory store a round's job left, for `melian records relay`, and refuses the batch whole before any record reaches a store. It walks the store's tree, refusing a link, another changeset's folder and any other file, and measures every file before it reads one: at most 512 files, 4 MiB a file, which is core's `recordLimit`, the most any store takes, and 8 MiB in all, twice that limit: one full record and as much again for the rest of the batch. It reads each folder one entry at a time and refuses past 2,048 entries in the whole walk, folders included, so a folder of a million empty folders costs it no more than the bound. A fork's batch holds check records only, and only of the checks `headCodeChecks` in `src/checks.ts` names, those that run the head's code; the job that holds the keys runs every other check itself. A writer's batch holds exactly one round at the run's revision, which names no walkthrough, sets no round aside, reads only records in the batch, and reads exactly one account. Every other record is triage, the round's telemetry or an early copy of a lens run it reads. At most 64 of those count, whether or not the round names them, and at most one triage record holds a decision. Telemetry is written after its round, so a round names none, and the relay refuses another round's telemetry whether the round names it or not. The account must be one `TierAccount.refusal` accepts, from the tier the caller loaded from the base and the facts the records it counts state: each check record's result, each lens record's check, the account's filled records, and triage's answers. The relay adds no proof of how a record came to be, by the maintainer's ruling of 2026-11-18.

The conformance suite asserts only that a refused record never lists and that a repeat of the rest completes the batch. Every adapter refuses a record whose canonical bytes pass `recordLimit`, 4 MiB of UTF-8, with `invalidRecord`, through `SharedRecord.storable()`, and measures the whole batch before it writes any of it; the conformance suite holds every adapter to that, at the limit and a byte past it. The relay takes a file up to the same limit, so the head's job never hands over a record no store keeps. A ruling on the limit changes that one number. A check record's sightings get the limit less `envelopeAllowance`, 4 KiB for the envelope and the check's result, as `SightingBudget.checkRecord`. Problem: a head that changes 1,500 workspace manifests, each naming twenty long scripts, writes a guardrails record of about 5 MB, and the store refuses it. Solution: `fit(findings)` walks the findings in ID order and keeps each one's detail while the full findings so far and the shortest form of every later one fit. Each later finding is `abridged(note)`: What becomes its fixed headline, unless its own What is shorter in UTF-8 bytes, Why here becomes "Melian left out the detail for N more files to keep this record under its limit; `git diff` shows those files.", with N the files those findings name, and its ID, rule, severity, resolution, place, snippet, trigger and What to do stay. A finding that abridging would not make smaller, because its Why here is shorter than the note, keeps its detail, so no finding grows. The same findings give the same bytes. When even every finding abridged does not fit, `fit` throws `RecordError` `recordTooLarge` with a fixed sentence, so the guardrails check fails and the review reads not reviewed, as [the decision](../decisions/2026-11-20-guardrails-record-fits-the-store.md) records. The cell holds one JSON value, and `writeCell` refuses any other with `invalidCell`. It sets no size bound: the decision calls a cell small and gives no number, and the build that defines the lease, [issue #396](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/issues/396), sets one. A `writeCell` that fails `unreachable` may have landed, as the git adapter's push stopped at its deadline may, so a repeat with the same expected version can answer `false` for the caller's own write. A caller that repeats one reads the cell, and a cell holding the value it wrote means its write landed. Only a value that names its writer, as a lease's incarnation does, tells the two apart; the publication lease is the first caller. Only `dispose` writes the disposal mark, `{"disposed":true}`, by compare-and-set over whatever the cell held; `writeCell` refuses that value with `invalidCell`. From then on `list` answers nothing, and `add` and `writeCell` throw `RecordError` `disposed`, so a record a dying `add` left after the mark never lists. A version is opaque and never reused: the memory adapter mints a random one on every write and the directory adapter numbers them, so a value that went away and came back never matches a version read before. That holds while only the store touches its own files. Someone who deletes a changeset's `.cell` directory by hand restarts the directory adapter's numbers at 1, so a version read before the deletion can match again. Only a writer with access to the store can do that, and rule 6 trusts such a writer. That writer could as easily rewrite the cell file itself, so the adapter does not guard against it.
